When games cost$ 50, we typically received a complete game and if players wanted to expand the games experience, we would purchase dlc. As time passed and games increased in production value, naturally the increased cost to create games was passed to the consumer and games are now around $60. Its been a while since games have jumped up in price but with the regular inclusion of microtransactions and on-disk dlc in future releases, the cost of a complete game winds up being $70+.

So I was wondering whether or not just bumping up the price of new games to $70-$75 would sort of decrease the presence of microtransactions as companies are receiving more money up front, thus putting more pressure on developers to put a more complete product and eliminate the need to lock a portion of a game behind a dlc wall.

What do you guys think?

Game companies just want to keep milking the cow in order to get more profit from their games.

For example: Call Of Duty Advancew Warfare

  • Game = $60

  • DLC map pack total of 4 = $15 x 4 = $60

Total $120 (not counting extra weapon skins and all of that)

Sadly, the audience for this game are teenagers and they are just so oblivious to these kind of Add-ons and they just think "Hey it's only $15" and the total price just keeps adding on.

If the base price is $70, some will be turned away for sure, but enough people will keep buying that soon $70 will become the new norm. It's called price creep, and it happens in just about every market.

A new Nintendo 64 game was $50 at launch. Per this calculator, that's already $72 today: http://www.usinflationcalculator.com/

I think he means that the value of the dollar is "going down." This is a byproduct of inflation and lowered interest rates.

You can think about it like a scale: You can buy (balance) a pound of bread, but you need a certain amount of dollars. But, if you make the value (or weight) of the dollar go down, you'll need more of them to buy that same amount of bread.

So, technically, the [value of the] dollar is going down.

Introduction

This guide serves as a reference of approximate card values. Knowing the values of cards is essential to fair trading.

 

Is this guide accurate?

Last updated: June 16 2015

All values in this guide are taken from The Top Cut. Read the “How are card values determined?” section of this guide for more information.

The values of cards from the most recent set (currently Roaring Skies) tend to change week-to-week. All other values tend to stay fairly constant. Most values decrease over time. However, even if this list is outdated, it should still serve as a good reference for relative values between cards.

I aim to update card values from the latest set weekly and to update all other values monthly.

If you want to ensure you have the most up-to-date values, do research yourself! Check to see how much cards are going for on the Public Trade boards in the PTCGO client (that is how all trading companies determine their prices).

 

My card is not listed – what to do?

This guide only lists –EX Pokemon and other SR cards, as they are the most common cards of which players wish to know the values. For a full list of all cards, search for your card at the official Top Cut Post (you have to log in).

 

How are card values determined?

Values are based on the listings of trading groups on the PTCGO forums. These groups are made of individual traders who “sell” cards at their listed prices.

All card values are based on current listings of the Public Trade board in the PTCGO client. However, due to the convenience of “ordering” from a trading group, their listed prices are typically 10%-50% higher than what a player would be able to get from Public Trading.

All values in this guide are obtained from The Top Cut (you have to log in). The Top Cut is the most commonly accepted source for card values. Other trading companies exist - if you wish to check them out, visit the Official Forums.

 

How are pack values determined?

Packs have different values, based on availability (supply) and popularity (demand). All values are listed in units of “standard packs.” The following table summarizes how many standard packs each pack type is worth, in terms of ratio of [pack] : [standard packs]. The values are only valid for 10-card unlocked (tradable) packs. All other packs are untradeable, and cannot be compared to tradable content.

Ratio Packs
0.10 : 1 HeartGold & SoulSilver, Unleashed, Undaunted, Triumphant, Call of Legends
0.67 : 1 Black and White
0.80 : 1 Noble Victories
0.90 : 1 Plasma Freeze
1.00 : 1 Boundaries Crossed, Dark Explorers, Dragon Vault, Next Destinies, Plasma Blast, Roaring Skies
1.25 : 1 Dragons Exalted, Plasma Storm
1.50 : 1 Furious Fists, Phantom Forces, Primal Clash, Double Crisis
2.00 : 1 Emerging Powers, FlashFire, Legendary Treasures, XY

Examples:

  1. Unleashed has a ratio of 0.10 : 1.
    • Thus 10 Unleashed packs = 100 standard packs.
  2. Roaring Skies has a ratio of 1.00 : 1.
    • Thus 10 Roaring Skies packs = 10 standard packs.
  3. FlashFire has a ratio of 2.00 : 1.
    • Thus 10 FlashFire packs = 5 standard packs.

 

How can I make fair trades with this guide?

Cards-for-Packs / Packs-for-Cards Trades: The “actual” values of all cards tabulated in this guide are likely worth slightly less than the values given. (This is due to the Trading Company’s “convenience inflation.”) Thus, for a fair trade, cards should usually be traded for 1-2 fewer packs than the values given in this guide.

Cards-for-Cards Trades: This guide gives fairly accurate price differences between individual cards. Thus, fair cards-for-cards trades should result in an equal value amount for players on both sides of the trade.

Example: Top Cut values a Full-Art Seismitoad-EX at 10 packs.

  1. You want to obtain this card by trading your packs.
    • You could offer 7-9 Roaring Skies packs on Public Trade and likely have your trade accepted.
  2. You want to obtain this card by trading your cards.
    • You could offer a Full-Art Gengar-EX (Top Cut value = 7 packs) and a Regular-Art Aggron-EX (Top Cut value = 3 packs) on Public Trade and likely have your trade accepted.
